analysis.one_liner: Expands free school meals and modernizes WIC nutrition aid for low-income families with children.
analysis.headline: The House committee approved the bill 27–20, but it never came up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would reauthorize and expand federal child nutrition programs, including school lunches and WIC aid for pregnant women, infants, and young children. It would let schools automatically enroll children in free meals through Medicaid, expand schools' ability to serve free meals to all students, raise the federal payment per school meal, and fund kitchen upgrades. It would also modernize WIC so children stay eligible through age six with two-year certification and less paperwork, create a summer grocery benefit for children, and limit penalties on kids with unpaid school meal debt.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income schoolchildren, who would get free meals more easily through Medicaid direct certification and expanded community eligibility; families on WIC, who would face shorter applications and longer certification periods; children who rely on school meals during summer, who would get a new grocery benefit; school cafeteria workers, whose required training would generally be scheduled during paid hours; and schools in low-income areas, which would get kitchen equipment and scratch-cooking grants.

how_it_helps.text: Lets schools certify children for free lunches and breakfasts automatically if they receive Medicaid and their family income is at or below 133% of the poverty line, with no household application needed.

Expands 'community eligibility': the formula for whole-school free meals would use a 2.5 multiplier and a lower 25% threshold, letting many more schools serve free meals to every student, with an option for statewide community eligibility.

Raises the federal reimbursement schools receive per meal (the base rate goes from 10.5 to 20.5 cents per lunch) and creates grant programs for scratch cooking and kitchen equipment upgrades, prioritizing schools serving the most low-income students.

Modernizes WIC: children could stay eligible through their sixth birthday or full-day kindergarten, certification periods would stretch to two years, applicants could enroll through Medicaid, SNAP, or Head Start without extra paperwork, and benefits could be redeemed online through EBT.
Creates a summer electronic grocery benefit for children who lose access to school meals when school is out, and expands the summer food service program.

Addresses 'lunch shaming' by setting rules around unpaid meal debt, and requires that required training for school food service workers be scheduled primarily during regular paid hours, with compensable pay if held outside them.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund the higher per-meal payments, expanded eligibility, the new summer grocery benefit, and the authorized grant programs; plus food companies that would face updated school nutrition standards and a required study and rulemaking on food service management contracts.

drawbacks.text: The bill would meaningfully increase federal spending: it raises the per-meal reimbursement, authorizes $20 million a year for scratch-cooking grants and $35 million a year for kitchen facilities through fiscal 2028, funds WIC technology at $90 million a year, and adds a new summer grocery benefit.

It gives the Secretary of Agriculture broad authority to waive nearly any requirement of the child nutrition programs during any declared emergency, on a statewide or nationwide basis, with waivers lasting 90 days beyond the emergency — a significant delegation with limited ongoing oversight.

Expanding community eligibility decouples free meals from individual family income: schools qualify based on a formula, so some free meals would go to children whose families could pay, raising the federal cost per meal served.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core design is a straightforward expansion of programs with documented reach: automatic enrollment cuts the paperwork that keeps eligible kids off the rolls, and the summer benefit fills a known gap. The real cost is federal money — tens of millions in authorized grants plus higher reimbursements and a new entitlement-style summer benefit. The loosest part is the sweeping emergency waiver authority, which trades oversight for flexibility. On the merits, the benefits to food-insecure children plausibly outweigh the fiscal cost, but none of it was enacted, so no family saw any of it.

outcome.mechanism: The committee passed the bill and put it on the House calendar, but House leaders never brought it up for a vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Scott introduced the bill on July 20, 2022, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
On July 27, 2022, the committee held a markup and voted 27–20 to report the bill with amendments.
On November 7, 2022, the committee formally reported the amended bill (H. Rept. 117-548) and it was placed on the Union Calendar, the queue of bills awaiting House floor action.
The House never took it up; the bill died on the calendar when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Child nutrition programs simply continued under existing rules. Contract school food companies and processed food makers avoided new scrutiny and standards, and taxpayers avoided the added spending — while the low-income families the bill was written for gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Food companies and existing programs, not hungry kids

industries.note: The bill orders a study and later a rule on the role of contract food companies in school meals — including contract practices, effects on cafeteria workers' pay, and use of funds to deter union organizing — and gives scratch-cooking grants priority to schools that run their own kitchens. That scrutiny and the self-operation preference threaten a business model built on taking over school food service, though it stops short of restricting it.

The bill directs updated school meal nutrition standards and specifically addresses non-nutritive sweeteners, synthetic dyes, and other potentially harmful substances in school meals. Companies selling those products into school cafeterias would face tighter requirements.

The bill requires states to let at least three vendors process WIC payments online by October 2025 and funds vendor-support programs, new business for retailers that invest in the systems. But it also changes the pricing benchmark WIC uses to judge vendor prices and tightens rules on stores charging above-average prices, squeezing margins for high-priced vendors.

The bill strengthens Buy American requirements for school food procurement, expands the farm-to-school grant program, and directs commodity purchases to emphasize domestic high-protein foods and seafood. More of the program's food dollars would flow to domestic producers.
